clue.text: Plans here for decentralizing school?

indicators.note: taking away the centre of something means its two middle letters are removed

parts.note: Charterhouse is an English public school in Surrey

explanation.surface: A question about where the plans for devolving a school's management are drawn up.
explanation.walkthrough: CHARTERHOUSE has twelve letters, so its centre is the sixth and seventh, ER; take them out and CHARTHOUSE remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A charthouse is the room on a ship where navigational charts, the vessel's plans of the sea, are kept.

clue.text: Many grew old in prison

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for many
to age is to grow old

explanation.surface: Plenty of people reached old age behind bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone caged is locked up behind bars, just as a prisoner is confined in a cell.

clue.text: Suddenly and simultaneously

definitions.meaning: second meaning: everything at the same moment

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means abruptly, as in a door slamming without warning, and also everyone acting together at one moment.

clue.text: Adam and I!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in Genesis, the original human being created
second meaning: the grammatical term for the pronoun of the speaker

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark hides how differently the two halves work: one is the Bible's first man, the other a term from grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam was the earliest human in Genesis, and the pronoun I is what grammarians call the speaker's own form.

clue.text: Some have a go at me — all I need in the Land of Cakes

definitions.text: Some have a go at me — all I need in the Land of Cakes

indicators.note: only some of the words that follow are used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across these words after the first G and before the final L

explanation.surface: A Scot invites people to try their food, saying it is all they need.
explanation.walkthrough: The Land of Cakes is an old nickname for Scotland, from its oatcakes; the whole clue is both the hiding place and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground oats are the Scottish staple behind porridge and oatcakes, the cakes that give that country its nickname.

clue.text: Simple skill needed in bridge

indicators.note: one thing needed inside another is placed within it

parts.note: a span is a bridge or the arch of one
art is skill or craft

explanation.surface: Playing the card game bridge only takes a little talent.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge looks like the card game, but it is a span over a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartan living is plain and austere, like the frugal ancient Greeks of Sparta, so the word means simple.

clue.text: Absorb liquid — not, by the sound of it, too drunk

indicators.note: telling us not to include something means it is taken out

parts.note: blotto is old slang for very drunk

indicators.note: the word is to be heard rather than read, standing for one spelt differently

parts.note: the preposition to is said the same as too

explanation.surface: Someone soaks up a spill and insists they are not too drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the sound of too, spelt TO, from the end of BLOTTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotting paper soaks up spilt ink, so to blot is to soak up a wet spill by pressing on it.

clue.text: Let down when 21 has a change heart of heart

indicators.text: has a change heart of heart
indicators.note: the middle letter of the word is swapped for a different one

parts.note: the answer to 21 across

explanation.surface: A sweetheart lets someone down by changing their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the V at the heart of LOVER for a W. The printed text repeats heart, an apparent misprint for a change of heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower something is to let it down, bringing it gently to a lesser height, as with a bucket on a rope.

clue.text: Sailor about to go round and round and live in Paddington, say

indicators.note: one thing about others goes around them on either side

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
water that eddies swirls round in circles
to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: A sailor spins about and settles in the London district of Paddington.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington looks like the London district and station, but it is the bear from Michael Bond's books; say marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddington Bear is a famous stuffed-toy character, so he is one example of a child's soft toy bear.

clue.text: Squashed alpaca kaftans out east

indicators.note: letters put out are knocked out of place and reformed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Woolly robes made of alpaca, worn out in the East, have been crushed.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something pressed completely level, as if it had been rolled under a heavy weight.

clue.text: Patience apparent in his work

parts.note: surface reading: a worker whose forbearance shows in everything he does
setter's reading: Patience is a comic opera, written by this librettist with Sullivan

explanation.walkthrough: Patience looks like a virtue, but with a capital it is the 1881 Savoy opera.
explanation.definitionFit: W S Gilbert wrote the words for the operetta Patience, one of the Savoy comic operas composed with Arthur Sullivan.

clue.text: Let, but nothing's been paid yet

definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: every penny still owing

explanation.surface: A property has been rented out, though the tenant has yet to pay anything.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer says the whole debt remains outstanding.
explanation.definitionFit: Allowed means permitted, and read as all owed it describes a debt where every penny remains outstanding.

clue.text: Terminated arrangement without a loss

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things into a new order
without means lacking, so something is left out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deal that was ended has left someone out of pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: Detriment is harm or damage suffered, so a loss in the general sense of being worse off.

clue.text: Hang about, waiting for feathers?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, said with a different vowel: smeared with tar, the first half of tarring and feathering

explanation.walkthrough: Tarring and feathering was a mob punishment: hot tar first, then feathers stuck to it, so someone covered in tar is waiting for the feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger or delay leaving, and the adjective, rhyming with starry, means coated in sticky black tar.

clue.text: Longs for underwear

definitions.meaning: first meaning: yearns, as in pining after something
second meaning: British word for knickers or underpants

explanation.walkthrough: Longs looks like long trousers, a hint at the garment, but it is a verb. In Britain pants are underwear, not trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pants after a thing yearns eagerly for it, and in British usage pants are underpants or knickers.

clue.text: Gambler loses head and becomes a thief

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a speculator gambles on markets

explanation.surface: A punter who has lost his nerve turns to crime.
explanation.definitionFit: A peculator embezzles money entrusted to him, so he is a thief of public or company funds.

clue.text: Picture head lights out of order

indicators.note: the two pieces are joined the other way round from the order in which they are clued

parts.note: a bird that lights on a branch lands there
a cape is a headland

explanation.surface: A car's broken headlights.
explanation.walkthrough: Headlights wants to be one word; split it, then put the second piece first.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape is a painting of countryside scenery, so it is a kind of picture.

clue.text: The claims he's made for transmutation!

definitions.text: The claims he's made for transmutation!

indicators.note: something made is fashioned anew from its materials

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Mocking the boasts of a man who says he can turn base metal into gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the letters are themselves transmuted.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval practitioner of this pseudo-science claimed he could turn lead into gold, the transmutation of metals.

clue.text: Lots leave drink unfinished outside in city street

indicators.note: something left outside goes around the other piece
not finished means the final letter is missing

parts.note: cider is an alcoholic apple drink
heaps means lots

explanation.surface: Drinkers abandon half-finished glasses outside a pub in town.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheapside is a historic street in the City of London, the financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapside is an old market street in the square mile of London, the area known as the City.

clue.text: Bill's in 22

parts.note: taken as written
the answer to 22 down

explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name; it is a demand for payment.
explanation.definitionFit: An invoice is a trader's itemised request for payment, the same thing as a bill.

clue.text: Sauce in some other shape

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed within it

parts.note: else means some other, as in somewhere else
sauce and lip both mean cheeky talk

explanation.surface: A condiment poured into a different kind of mould.
explanation.walkthrough: Sauce looks like a condiment, but it is impudence.
explanation.definitionFit: An ellipse is an oval, a geometric figure like a flattened circle, and so a shape.

clue.text: Park sign, a maple-tree — for one who walks here

parts.note: P is the road-sign symbol for a car park
Acer is the botanical name of the maple

explanation.surface: Signs in a park point out a maple to anyone strolling past.
explanation.walkthrough: Here points back at the wordplay: the letters spell out the one who walks.
explanation.definitionFit: A pacer walks with measured steps, pacing to and fro, or sets the speed for others on foot.

clue.text: Gallant leaders of revolution given backing

indicators.note: going backwards means the letters are read from right to left
the leaders are the front part, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The heads of an uprising are given support.
explanation.walkthrough: Leaders here are the first five letters of one word, not the first letters of several.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallant is an old word for a dashing man who courts women, a suitor or admirer.

clue.text: Express love, instead of concealing it

indicators.note: something concealing another holds it out of sight inside

parts.note: vice is Latin for in place of, as in vice-captain
love is zero in tennis, and zero looks like O

explanation.surface: Someone declares love openly rather than hiding it.
explanation.walkthrough: It refers back to love, the piece being hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: To voice a feeling is to say it out loud, putting it into words, which is what express means.

clue.text: Offer 21 tune changes

indicators.note: a change of these letters puts them in a fresh order

parts.note: the answer to 21 across
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suitor adjusts his serenade.
explanation.definitionFit: To volunteer is to put yourself forward or proffer something freely, without being asked.

clue.text: Mat, a boy with no love for sport

parts.note: a rug is a small mat

indicators.note: having none of something means it is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A lad who is unloved turns to a doormat for company.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby is a team ball game played with an oval ball, named after the English school where it began.

clue.text: In port, I look back on voyage

parts.note: a trip is a journey

indicators.note: looking back means the letters are taken in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: A sailor in harbour thinks back over the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: On voyage means the letters follow the voyage piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli, capital of Libya, is a harbour city on the Mediterranean coast, and so a port.

clue.text: Ringing the changes with vegetable and fish

parts.note: a pea is a vegetable
ling is a fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Varying a menu of vegetables and fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Ringing the changes sounds like varying things, but here it is bell-ringing.
explanation.definitionFit: Change ringing is the English art of sounding church bells in shifting sequences, so ringing the changes is bells pealing.

clue.text: A hazard to sailors — I'd say not

parts.note: surface reading: a rock or sandbank lying just below the water that can wreck a ship
setter's reading: not said out loud is knot, and sailors tie a square knot named after this word, which is no hazard at all

explanation.walkthrough: The second half sounds like a denial, but spoken it is knot: the same word names a square knot sailors tie, so the hazard is also a sailor's tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridge of rock or coral near the sea surface is a classic danger to shipping, ripping open hulls that run onto it.

clue.text: Relent, very unusually and respectfully

indicators.note: something done unusually departs from its normal order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone gives way, surprisingly, and with deference.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting reverently means showing deep respect or awe, as in a church or before a revered person.
